summary:
Scotland stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 framework, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The practical result for a trans visitor in Scotland is that facilities designated by biological sex are the ones to be used, with organisations instructed on how to enforce that division lawfully.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. That guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The competing arguments were aired in the same court on 5 February 2026, when government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard against suicide risk and For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Searching and strip-searching in Scottish custody follows the same principle. On 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance under which custody searches and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with an effort made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police adopted an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth, replacing a prior policy that had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate.

Gender recognition documents carry entry consequences. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. Within the United Kingdom a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents, and where the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated.

Scotland's own enforcement picture sits on top of that framework. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported 7,115 hate-crime charges in 2025-26, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up from 86 and the highest level recorded since the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 took effect; sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25 in the first annual report under the 2021 Act, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each. Sixty-two per cent of those recorded offences carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator.
tangentialFactors:
Restrictions on trans minors run through the parent framework. NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Cass Review of April 2024 also led NHS England to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. Bell v Tavistock of December 2020 had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers, a judgment overturned on appeal in September 2021.

Schools and sport carry parallel bars. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010.

On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people. Northern Ireland, which sits on different equality legislation, is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling, so the position north of the Scottish border may diverge from the rules described here.

The December 2023 refusal to recognise foreign gender recognition certificates drew political division: the Women and Equalities Minister, Kemi Badenoch, called the changes long overdue, while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Transgender people seeking a UK certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first where a spouse withholds consent.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Scottish Prison Service has issued replacement trans-custody guidance following the Court of Session ruling of 19 June 2026 is not sourced here, and the terms of any such replacement are unresolved.

How the single-sex spaces code of August 2026 interacts with devolved equality competence in Scotland, and whether Scottish bodies received separate guidance from the equality watchdog, is not addressed in the available material.

Access to gender-affirming care for adults in Scotland is not sourced. The care restrictions described in the parent framework come from NHS England decisions and NHS England reporting; the corresponding position of NHS Scotland for adults and for minors is not stated in the inventory.

The Crown Office figures are charges rather than convictions, and the inventory does not give outcomes, breakdowns by victim gender identity, or the number of aggravated cases that proceeded to trial. The police-recorded 2024-25 figures likewise do not disaggregate victims by transgender status.

The exact date on which the equality watchdog's code took effect in August 2026 is not specified in the source material.
